subject: anatomy
title: Plantar Aponeurosis, Longitudinal Arches, and Foot Deformities

steps.tx: The **plantar aponeurosis** is a dense, glistening triangular sheet of deep fascia situated in the central sole of the foot. Attached posteriorly to the medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity, it broadens distally into five longitudinal digital slips that insert into the fibrous flexor sheaths and bases of the proximal phalanges.
steps.say: The plantar aponeurosis is a tough fibrous sheet covering the central sole. Attached posteriorly to the calcaneal tuberosity, it splits distally into five digital slips inserting onto the proximal phalanges.

steps.tx: The plantar aponeurosis functions as a dynamic mechanical tie-rod, acting through the **windlass mechanism** described by Hicks. Dorsiflexion of the toes during terminal stance winds the digital slips around the metatarsal heads, pulling the calcaneus towards the forefoot, elevating the medial longitudinal arch, and converting the foot into a rigid lever for push-off.
steps.say: The plantar aponeurosis operates through the windlass mechanism. During toe dorsiflexion at push-off, its slips wind over the metatarsal heads, shortening the tie-rod and stiffening the arch into a rigid propulsion lever.

steps.tx: Microtrauma and repetitive tensile traction at the calcaneal origin of the plantar aponeurosis provoke **plantar fasciitis**, the most common cause of heel pain in adults. Patients report severe, lancinating heel pain with the first steps in the morning or following periods of rest, localized to the anteromedial calcaneal tuberosity.
steps.say: Repetitive tensile overload at the calcaneal insertion causes plantar fasciitis. Patients experience sharp heel pain on taking the first morning steps, pinpointed over the anteromedial calcaneus.

steps.tx: The intrinsic muscles of the sole are arranged in four orderly layers. The first layer consists of abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, and abductor digiti minimi; the second layer contains the **quadratus plantae** (which aligns the oblique pull of FDL) and four lumbricals; the third layer contains short flexors and adductor hallucis; the fourth contains interossei.
steps.say: The muscles of the sole form four layers. The second layer contains quadratus plantae and four lumbricals. Quadratus plantae attaches into flexor digitorum longus to straighten its oblique traction vector.

steps.tx: The foot architecture incorporates three arches that absorb shock and transmit body weight: the medial longitudinal arch, lateral longitudinal arch, and **transverse arch**. The medial longitudinal arch is the higher and more elastic arch, composed of the calcaneus, talus (keystone), navicular, three cuneiforms, and medial three metatarsals.
steps.say: The foot features medial longitudinal, lateral longitudinal, and transverse arches. The medial arch is higher and more elastic, supported by the talar keystone, navicular, cuneiforms, and first three metatarsals.

steps.tx: The critical ligamentous support of the medial arch is the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament, universally termed the **spring ligament**. Extending from the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus to the plantar surface of the navicular, it directly cradles the rounded head of the talus, preventing its downward and medial collapse.
steps.say: The spring ligament is the primary ligamentous brace of the medial arch. Connecting the sustentaculum tali to the navicular, it forms an elastic socket supporting the head of the talus.

steps.tx: Failure of the spring ligament or insufficiency of the tibialis posterior tendon causes flattening of the medial longitudinal arch, designated **pes planus** (flatfoot). Conversely, pathological elevation of the longitudinal arch occurs in pes cavus, seen in hereditary motor sensory neuropathies (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease) and Friedreich ataxia due to intrinsic-extrinsic muscle imbalance.
steps.say: Insufficiency of the spring ligament or tibialis posterior tendon leads to flatfoot, termed pes planus. Conversely, abnormally high arches characterize pes cavus, seen in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.

steps.tx: Arterial perfusion of the dorsal foot is delivered by the **dorsalis pedis artery**, the continuation of the anterior tibial artery at the midpoint between the malleoli. Passing along the medial border of the dorsum, its pulsation is palpated against the navicular and cuneiform bones immediately lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus.
steps.say: The dorsalis pedis artery delivers blood to the dorsal foot as the continuation of the anterior tibial artery. Its pulse is palpated between the malleoli lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.
